monthly.fieldTitle: Weigh your bird every day: What a gram scale tells you before your parrot does
monthly.fieldDek: Weight is the first honest signal of a parrot's health. Why daily weighing matters, what normal fluctuation looks like, and when the trend means call the vet.
monthly.reply: What have your birds been up to? Reply and tell me. Every one comes straight to me.
monthly.healthNote: This app doesn't diagnose illness. If you're ever worried about your bird's health, contact an avian veterinarian.
monthly.foot: You're getting this because you have a Kya & Co. account. You can turn off the monthly letter in Settings at any time.
monthly.q.lead: A new month is an easy place to pick things back up. One weight is enough to start again, and everything you logged before is still on the record.
monthly.q.start1: Log a weight. It takes about a minute, and it picks the trend up where you left it.
monthly.q.start2: Run a health check. A few questions about how your bird looks and behaves today.

1.alt: A sun conure looking over its shoulder
1.title: Book the wellness visit
notes: Put a date on the calendar. A yearly check with an avian vet gives you both a baseline to compare against, even when everything seems fine.
Bring the record. Open the vet summary before you go and jot down anything you've been wondering about, however small.
Practice the carrier. A few short, calm visits to the carrier in the weeks before make the trip easier on everyone.

2.alt: A white cockatoo with a yellow crest, holding food in one foot
2.title: Make food take a bit of work
notes: Start easy. Wrap a favorite treat loosely in plain paper, or tuck it into a paper cup. The first puzzle should be one your bird can solve.
Build up slowly. Once your bird has the idea, try a foraging toy, or hide pieces of the usual food around the cage.
Keep an eye on the bowl. Make sure your bird is still eating enough while they learn. Their weight trend will tell you if something's shifted.

3.alt: A golden conure perched on a bare branch
3.title: Look after their feet
notes: Mix up the perches. Different widths and textures let feet work in different ways. Natural branches from bird-safe wood are a good place to start.
Check for wear. Look for loose fittings, cracks, and smooth, worn spots, and replace anything that's seen better days.
Watch how they stand. In a calm moment, notice how your bird grips and balances. If something looks different from usual, ask your vet.

4.alt: A rainbow lorikeet preening its tail feathers on a rope perch
4.title: Make time for a bath
notes: Offer a few options. Some birds love a shallow dish, some prefer a light mist, and some would rather sit with you near the shower.
Keep it warm and easy. Lukewarm water, a warm room, and plenty of time to dry off afterward.
Let your bird decide. If they're not interested today, try again another day. Note what they like in the journal.

5.alt: A green eclectus parrot on a thin branch among leaves
5.title: Give the toy box a once-over
notes: Check what you have. Fraying rope, loose parts, and cracked plastic are worth replacing before they become a problem.
Rotate a few. Put some toys away and bring back ones your bird hasn't seen in a while. Old favorites often feel new again.
Notice what gets chewed. Which toys get destroyed and which get ignored is a good clue for what to offer next.

6.alt: A green parrot with an orange face perched in a leafy tree
6.title: Add something new to the bowl
notes: Try one new vegetable. Offer it more than once. Many parrots need to see a food several times before they'll taste it.
Change the shape. Chopped, whole, grated, or threaded on a skewer can each land differently.
Ask about the balance. The right mix of pellets, fresh food, and seed depends on species, so it's a good question for your next vet visit.

7.alt: A close-up of a green conure with red markings on its face
7.title: Do a gentle once-over
notes: Pick a calm moment. Sitting close during a quiet time is enough. There's no need to hold your bird still.
Look at nails, beak, and eyes. You're learning what's usual for your bird, so a change stands out later.
Write down what you see. A short journal note, and a photo if you can, gives you something to compare next time. If something has changed, ask your vet.

8.alt: A green budgerigar perched in front of a dark aviary
8.title: Get ready for the unexpected
notes: Fill in the Emergency section. Add your avian vet, the nearest emergency clinic, and who to call if you can't be reached.
Keep a carrier ready. Somewhere easy to reach, with a towel and a small container of food.
Share the plan. Make sure anyone who helps with your bird knows where to find it.

9.alt: An African grey parrot looking up from a red perch indoors
9.title: Keep the air clean at home
notes: Be careful with nonstick pans. Overheated nonstick cookware can release fumes that are very dangerous to birds. Keep your bird well away from the kitchen when you cook.
Go easy on scents. Aerosol sprays, scented candles, plug-in air fresheners, and strong cleaning products are best kept away from where your bird spends time.
Let fresh air in. Open a window when you clean or cook, and keep your bird in another room until the air clears.

10.alt: A white cockatiel with orange cheeks beside a wooden nest box
10.title: Protect a good night's sleep
notes: Keep bedtime steady. A regular time, a dark room, and quiet help most parrots settle.
Notice what wakes them. Late TV, passing headlights, or a busy hallway can interrupt sleep more than you'd think.
Write down the routine. Add bedtime to the Routine section of the care plan so anyone helping out keeps it the same.

11.alt: Two hyacinth macaws sitting close together on a rope
11.title: Spend a few minutes on training
notes: Keep sessions short. A few minutes at a time, ending while your bird is still interested.
Start with something simple. Stepping up, or touching a target stick, builds trust and makes everyday care easier.
Reward what you want to see. A favorite treat and your attention go a long way. Note progress in the journal.

12.alt: A green macaw with a red forehead perched in an aviary
12.title: Plan for a busy house
notes: Keep the basics steady. Meals, sleep, and time out of the cage matter more when the house is full or the routine shifts.
Give your bird a quiet spot. Somewhere calm to retreat to when there are guests, noise, or new things around.
Watch for hazards. Open doors, candles, decorations, and unfamiliar foods are worth an extra look.
